meta.title: Classification — Source × Type × Pattern
meta.sub: You leave this session with: Chapter 3 — what KIND of innovation this is, and what that implies

moves.detail: Read Ch. 3 of the Carmen Market study — and its last line especially.
Three frameworks, three lines, no notes.
Tech-push or market-pull? Use the deciding question.
Incremental or disruptive? Use the anchor test.
Write the consequence line. Peer check.

model.label: THE MODEL — how the Carmen Market study did it
model.html:
Source: Market-Pull with a tech-push assist · Type: Incremental · Pattern: Application

And then the line that actually matters: “Because it is Incremental + Application, the realistic budget and timeline are small, and the main risk is adoption failure, not technical failure.”

Classification is not a labelling exercise. It tells you what your Chapter 7 budget and Chapter 8 risks should look like before you write them.

steps.label: STEP 1 — Source
steps.instruction: The deciding question, from Week 2: what problem existed BEFORE this technology was built?

options.note: Careful — tech-push means the technology existed first and someone went looking for a problem to apply it to. Make sure your problem sentence (Chapter 1) really did come after the tech, not before it.
The problem existed first and people were already looking for a fix — this is the more common, and usually more defensible, answer for a course problem you diagnosed yourself.

Only choose this if you can name both halves separately: the pre-existing problem AND the pre-existing technology that got pointed at it. 'Hybrid' used as a way to avoid deciding is a trap, not an analysis.

steps.label: STEP 1 (cont.) — Source, the reason
steps.instruction: State it plainly — this is what your circled answer above has to be defensible against.
steps.prefix: The problem that existed first was:

steps.label: STEP 2 — Type
steps.instruction: The anchor test, from Week 3: does this make an ENTIRE old category obsolete, or does it just improve one thing?

options.note: The old way still exists and still works for some people — you're improving one thing, not ending a category. This is the far more common, and far more honest, answer.

Careful — this is a description, not a compliment. Apply the anchor test: does an ENTIRE old category go obsolete because of this? If you can't name what specifically becomes obsolete, claiming 'disruptive' will make your Ch. 7 budget nonsense.

steps.label: STEP 2 (cont.) — Type, the reason
steps.instruction: Name the specific old category, or state plainly that nothing goes obsolete.
steps.prefix: What becomes obsolete — or what does not:

steps.label: STEP 3 — Pattern
steps.instruction: Improvement = same tool, same place, done better. Application = existing tool, moved somewhere new. Recombination = two or more existing things fused.

options.note: Same tool, same place, just done better. Check this is really true — if you moved the tool somewhere it wasn't used before, that's Application, not Improvement.
An existing tool, moved somewhere new. This is the Carmen Market study's own answer — check whether your case fits the same shape: nothing new invented, just redeployed.
Two or more existing things fused into one. Make sure you can name both existing pieces separately — if you can't, you may be describing Application instead.

steps.label: STEP 4 — The consequence line
steps.instruction: This is the whole point of the chapter. Complete the sentence honestly.
steps.prefix: Because we classified this as ______________ + ______________, our budget should be roughly ______________ and our biggest risk is ______________ failure — not ______________ failure.

trap.label: THE TRAP
trap.html: Two traps here. First: ‘disruptive’ sounds like a compliment, so teams reach for it — it is not a grade, it is a description, and claiming it wrongly will make your Chapter 7 budget nonsense. Second: teams treat this chapter as three labels to tick and move on. If your classification does not change what you write in Chapters 7 and 8, you have not actually done Chapter 3.

peer_check.label: PEER CHECK
peer_check.instruction: Swap with another team. Their job is not to be nice — it is to find the specific weakness named below.
peer_check.task: Read their consequence line. Then ask: ‘if you had classified this the OPPOSITE way, what number in your budget would change?’ If they cannot answer, their classification is decoration, not reasoning.

file_it.label: FILE IT
file_it.instruction: Date it, initial it, and add it to your team's dossier folder. A chapter that is not filed does not exist.
